properties.name: Ambiq — SPOT Subthreshold Power Platform
properties.description:
**Ambiq — SPOT Subthreshold Power Platform** — Ambiq Micro, Inc., Austin, TX (US)

Ambiq builds ultra-low-power SoCs around SPOT (Subthreshold Power Optimized Technology), operating transistors below 1V -- as low as 300mV in its newest 12nm platform -- for a quadratic energy-efficiency gain over conventional above-threshold digital design. Has shipped in over 280 million devices (wearables, healthcare monitoring, industrial IoT); latest product is Atomiq, an ultra-low-power NPU SoC.

[[https://ambiq.com/technology/spot/|Group website]]

Category: Electronic Engineering (Chip) Lab · Smallest demonstrated: unknown

properties.name: Molnar Group
properties.description:
**Alyosha Molnar** — Cornell University, Ithaca, NY (US)

Bioelectronics
Maker of Purcell Bot, Ant-Bot, Dog-Bot
Worked with McEuen and Miskin


Our group works primarily in a space encompassing integrated circuits for RF, computational imaging, and bioelectrical interfaces under the direction of Dr. Alyosha Molnar. As a result, we have had to develop a range of expertise, from signal processing algorithms to systems architecture to transistor-level circuits to opto-electronic device physics to wet biology (and especially neurobiology). This broad range of interests is rooted in core expertise in radio communications circuits and sensory (and especially visual) neuroscience. One of the great things about interdisciplinary research is that reveals fundamental similarities across problems, and so spurs new interdisciplinary research in unexpected directions. We are often confused, but rarely bored.

[[https://molnargroup.ece.cornell.edu/|Group website]]

properties.name: CSEM -- Analog Front-Ends for Implantable Devices
properties.description:
**CSEM -- Analog Front-Ends for Implantable Devices** — CSEM (Centre Suisse d'Electronique et de Microtechnique), Neuchâtel (CH)

CSEM designs custom ultra-low-power analog front-end ASICs for wearable and implantable medical devices -- multi-channel systems for brain, heart, and muscle monitoring, and specialized circuits for invasive epilepsy treatment and neural brain-machine interfaces. Focus is on minimizing power consumption to extend implant battery life while maintaining precise biomedical signal acquisition.

[[https://www.csem.ch/en/technical-focus/asics-for-the-edge/analog-front-ends/|Group website]]

properties.name: Fraunhofer ENAS
properties.description:
**Fraunhofer ENAS** — Fraunhofer Institute for Electronic Nano Systems, Chemnitz (DE)

Develops smart integrated systems using micro and nano technologies: individual components, manufacturing technologies, system concepts, and system integration, from initial idea through design, technology development, prototyping, and technology transfer. Its Nano Device Technologies department works on multidimensional, highly sensitive magnetic field sensors based on GMR and TMR effects. Located on the Smart Systems Campus, directly adjacent to Chemnitz University of Technology, and cooperates with the university's Center for Microtechnologies (ZfM).

[[https://www.enas.fraunhofer.de/en.html|Group website]]

properties.description:
**Muhannad Bakir** — Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA (US)

Researches 2.5D and 3D chip packaging integration architectures, co-designing thermal management, power delivery, and interconnect technologies to combine diverse chip types (digital, analog, photonic) into a single system. Applications named include healthcare systems alongside machine learning and autonomous vehicles. Part of Georgia Tech's broader 3D Systems Packaging Research Center.

[[https://bakirlab.gatech.edu/|Group website]]

properties.name: HaiLa Technologies
properties.description:
**HaiLa Technologies** — HaiLa Technologies Inc., Montreal, QC (CA)

Fabless semiconductor company building passive backscatter wireless SoCs -- the BSC2000, the first monolithic chip implementing passive backscatter on Wi-Fi, and the in-development BSC3000 combining backscatter with an active RISC-V-based transceiver. Removes the need for battery maintenance by reflecting ambient wireless signals instead of generating RF actively. Founded 2019, originally conceptualized at Stanford.

[[https://www.haila.io/|Group website]]

properties.name: Ilika — Stereax Solid-State Batteries
properties.description:
**Ilika — Stereax Solid-State Batteries** — Ilika plc, Romsey (GB)

UK company making Stereax, mm-scale solid-state rechargeable batteries for active medical implants and miniature IoT sensors -- no liquid or polymer components, thousands of recharge cycles, nA-level leakage. The Stereax M50 is a 20 mm3 rectangular-form-factor cell with 50% higher energy density than other commercial solid-state batteries.

[[https://www.ilika.com/micro-solid-state-batteries|Group website]]

properties.name: Rogers Research Group
properties.description:
**John A. Rogers** — Northwestern University, Evanston, IL (US)

Pioneers bioresorbable and flexible electronics -- implants that deliver wireless electrical stimulation to damaged nerves during healing, then dissolve and disappear without a trace ('bioresorbable electronic medicine'). Also develops soft, stretchable microfluidic systems that bond to skin without irritation. PI John A. Rogers directs Northwestern's Querrey-Simpson Institute for Bioelectronics.

[[https://rogersgroup.northwestern.edu/|Group website]]

properties.name: Arbabian Lab
properties.description:
**Amin Arbabian** — Stanford University, Stanford, CA (US)

Designs ultrasonically-powered implantable medical devices, targeting the problem of delivering 100s of µW to a few mW to millimeter and sub-millimeter implants located more than 10 cm deep in the body. Applications include pressure sensing, electrical stimulation, drug delivery, imaging, and optogenetics; a recent fully packaged device measures 30.5 mm³.

properties.name: WiBotic
properties.description:
**Ben Waters** — WiBotic Inc., Seattle, WA (US)

Spun out of the University of Washington in 2015, WiBotic builds adaptive resonant inductive wireless charging systems that let autonomous robots, drones, and marine vehicles recharge without manual plug-in. Founded by Ben Waters (UW EE PhD) and Professor Joshua Smith; the underlying wireless power technology was originally developed to power an LVAD (left ventricular assist device) heart pump without transcutaneous cables.

[[https://www.wibotic.com/|Group website]]
